description: Religion as Britain's established faith; secularisation and humanism; clashes with secular law and medical ethics.
content_html:
Religion and the State in Britain

Britain is unusual among modern democracies in having an established religion — the Church of England. The Monarch is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England, a title established by Elizabeth I’s Act of Supremacy in 1559 (Henry VIII’s 1534 Act had made him “Supreme Head”, a title Elizabeth deliberately softened to “Supreme Governor”). This means Christianity is woven into the fabric of British public life in ways that are often invisible until they are contested.

The most visible sign of this is in Parliament: Church of England bishops — known as the Lords Spiritual — sit in the House of Lords and can vote on legislation. Twenty-six senior bishops currently hold these seats, including the Archbishops of Canterbury and York. Critics argue this gives one religion an undemocratic privilege in a multi-faith society; supporters say the bishops bring a moral and pastoral voice that purely party-political peers may lack.

Beyond Parliament, the Church provides services that touch all citizens: church schools educate roughly a quarter of all state primary pupils in England; religious services mark national events such as royal funerals, state openings of Parliament, and Remembrance Sunday; and public holidays such as Christmas and Easter reflect the Christian calendar. These arrangements are often called “soft establishment” — the legal and cultural intertwining of Christianity with state identity.

Key Fact

The Monarch is Supreme Governor of the Church of England; Church of England bishops sit in the House of Lords; church schools educate roughly a quarter of state primary pupils in England; and public holidays such as Christmas and Easter reflect the Christian calendar.

Secularisation: The Decline of Religion’s Public Role

Secularisation describes the long-term shift in which religion becomes less central to how societies organise themselves and how individuals make decisions. In Britain, church attendance has fallen sharply since the 1950s: the 2021 census was the first in which fewer than half of respondents described themselves as Christian. The sociologist Steve Bruce argues that modernisation — through science, individualism and social pluralism — inevitably weakens religious authority.

Secularisation affects religion in several overlapping ways. Institutional secularisation means that laws, schools and hospitals are no longer controlled by religious bodies. Individual secularisation means that people make ethical decisions — about divorce, sexuality or end-of-life care — without consulting religious teaching. Cultural secularisation means that religious symbols, language and festivals lose their original meaning and become largely commercial (as many argue has happened to Christmas).

The Education Act of 1988 required all state schools to hold a daily act of collective worship that was “wholly or mainly of a broadly Christian character.” This remains law today, though many schools do not fully comply. The Act also made Religious Education compulsory — though parents retain the right to withdraw children.

This creates a genuine tension. Secularists and humanists argue that imposing Christian worship on children of all backgrounds in a diverse society is both unfair and counterproductive. Faith groups and many Christians argue that introducing children to religious reflection — even broadly — builds moral character and cultural literacy. The existence of faith schools sharpens this debate: state-funded schools run by religious bodies can, within limits, prioritise admission of pupils from their own faith community, teach from a faith perspective, and appoint staff on religious grounds.

Humanism: An Alternative Worldview

Humanism is not simply the absence of religion — it is a positive worldview with its own values, methods and organisations. In Britain, Humanists UK (formerly the British Humanist Association) represents and campaigns for people who hold a naturalistic, reason-based view of the world. Humanists believe that human beings are capable of determining right and wrong through reason and empathy alone, without needing divine commands or sacred texts.

Humanists support a fully secular state: they argue that laws should be based on evidence and the common good, not on the teachings of any one religion. They have campaigned for the removal of bishops from the House of Lords, for an end to compulsory acts of worship in schools, and for inclusive sex education. The National Secular Society takes a similar position, arguing for a strict separation of religion and state. The Sunday Assembly — sometimes called the “atheist church” — offers community gatherings with music, reflection and speakers, meeting the social functions that many people find in religion without any supernatural beliefs.

Key Fact

Humanists UK (formerly the British Humanist Association) campaigns for a fully secular state: removal of bishops from the Lords, ending compulsory school worship, and inclusive relationships education. The National Secular Society and Sunday Assembly pursue related goals from secular perspectives.

Religion, Law and Equality

Some of the sharpest conflicts between religious teaching and secular law arise over equality and family law. The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation, race, and religion or belief. For most religious organisations, this presents no difficulty — they have long-standing commitments to fairness and human dignity. However, tensions arise when religious teaching appears to conflict with protected characteristics.

The most discussed example is same-sex marriage. The Church of England and the Catholic Church in England and Wales teach that marriage is between a man and a woman — a view they ground in scripture (for instance, Exodus 20:13 and broader creation theology) and natural law. The state legalised same-sex civil marriage in 2014. Religious organisations were given an explicit exemption: they are not required to conduct same-sex marriages. However, some Christians argue that even operating within a society where same-sex marriage is legal creates moral difficulty.

Forced and arranged marriages create a different kind of tension. Arranged marriages — where families introduce partners but both parties freely consent — are not illegal and are practised in many religious communities. Forced marriages, where consent is absent, are a criminal offence. Religious communities themselves have often been vocal in condemning forced marriage; the tension is not between religion and law but between genuine religious practice and abuse carried out in a religious context. The government’s Forced Marriage Unit works with community leaders, including imams and Hindu community representatives, to address the issue.

Medical ethics is another arena where religious and secular values regularly clash. Most religious traditions assert the sanctity of human life from conception, grounding this in texts such as Psalm 139:13 (“you knit me together in my mother’s womb”) and Exodus 20:13 (“You shall not murder”). This leads many Christians, Muslims, and members of other faiths to oppose euthanasia and to restrict their acceptance of abortion. Secular ethicists often prioritise self-determination — the idea that individuals should have control over their own bodies and end-of-life choices.

Genetic manipulation raises questions about the creation of life and the limits of human intervention in natural processes. Therapeutic gene editing — correcting inherited diseases — receives more cautious religious support than the creation of “designer babies” selected for non-medical traits. Humanists tend to support medical advances that reduce suffering; the key question for them is whether the science is safe and used fairly, not whether it violates divine intentions. Religious objectors argue that such techniques treat human embryos as raw material, undermining their inherent dignity.

Key Concepts: Tolerance and Freedom

Underlying all these debates are competing understandings of tolerance, freedom of belief, freedom of expression, and freedom of practice. In a plural society, these freedoms are in constant negotiation. Religious believers ask for the freedom to live according to their convictions, including in public and professional life. Secularists ask that no one worldview — including any particular religion — be given privileged authority over others. The question of whether secular values should take precedence over religious values — or whether a genuine dialogue between them is possible — is central to this theme.
exam_tip_html: This theme is AO2-weighted (60%), so examiners are looking for reasoned evaluation, not just description. For “Explain” questions (6 marks), name a specific organisation or law — for example, the Education Act 1988 or Humanists UK — and explain its significance. For the 15-mark “Discuss” question, always present at least two developed perspectives and reach a justified conclusion. A common mistake is treating “secularism” as the same as “atheism” — secularism is a political principle about the separation of religion and state, not a claim about God’s existence. On the extended response, accurate spelling of technical terms such as “secularisation”, “euthanasia”, and “humanism” is rewarded in the SPaG marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Britain has an established religion (the Church of England): the Monarch is Supreme Governor, bishops sit in the House of Lords, and church schools educate roughly a quarter of state primary pupils.
  • Secularisation describes the process by which religion loses social significance; it is institutional, individual and cultural. The Education Act 1988 required broadly Christian collective worship in state schools — a continued point of tension.
  • Humanists UK, the National Secular Society, and the Sunday Assembly represent organised non-religious voices advocating for a fully secular state and inclusive, reason-based ethics.
  • Key clash-points between religious and secular values include equality law and same-sex marriage, forced and arranged marriages, and medical ethics (euthanasia, abortion, genetic manipulation). The concepts of tolerance, freedom of belief, and self-determination sit at the heart of these debates.

practice_questions.marks: Supreme Governor of the Church of England. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by secularisation.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: the process by which religion loses social significance / influence over public life (1 mark); reference to declining church attendance, changing laws or reduced role of religion in institutions (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Church of England is part of British public life.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each (up to 3) for any of: bishops in the House of Lords / Lords Spiritual; the Monarch as Supreme Governor of the Church of England; church schools educating roughly a quarter of state primary pupils; public holidays such as Christmas and Easter reflecting the Christian calendar; national services of thanksgiving or mourning held in churches; the Education Act 1988 requiring broadly Christian collective worship in state schools. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which religious and secular values may clash over medical ethics.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Responses may include:
• Euthanasia: many Christians and Muslims oppose assisted dying on the grounds that life is sacred (Exodus 20:13; Psalm 139:13) and only God should determine when life ends. Secular ethicists and Humanists argue that self-determination means individuals should control end-of-life decisions.
• Abortion: religious traditions often teach that life begins at conception, making abortion morally equivalent to taking life. Secular law in Britain permits abortion up to 24 weeks, prioritising the woman’s autonomy.
• Genetic manipulation: religious objectors argue that embryo selection treats human life as raw material, violating human dignity. Humanists tend to support therapeutic gene editing that reduces suffering, provided it is safe and fairly used.
[6 marks — 3 marks per clash: 1 for identifying the issue, 2 for explaining the religious view, 3 for including a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: '‘Britain should be a fully secular state, with no special role for religion in public life.’ Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• In a multi-faith and increasingly non-religious society, privileging one religion (Christianity) in law and Parliament is undemocratic. The 2021 census recorded fewer than half of people identifying as Christian for the first time.
• Humanists UK and the National Secular Society argue that state neutrality on religion protects all citizens equally, whether believers, agnostics or atheists.
• The Education Act 1988 requirement for broadly Christian worship in state schools is outdated in a diverse society; secular collective assemblies would include all pupils equally.
• Equality law requires equal treatment regardless of religion; having bishops in the Lords gives one faith group preferential political access.

Arguments against:
• The Church of England provides social infrastructure (schools, food banks, chaplaincy in hospitals and prisons) that benefits the whole country, not just Christians. Removing its establishment could reduce this contribution.
• The Lords Spiritual bring pastoral and moral perspectives to legislation that purely party-political peers may lack. Many bishops have championed social justice causes.
• Religious freedom includes the freedom of communities to express their values publicly and for religion to have a voice in national debate. A fully secular state could silence legitimate religious perspectives.
• The Christian heritage of Britain has shaped its democratic values, common law and welfare tradition; severing this connection could undermine rather than strengthen shared identity.

Mastering (13–15 marks): Both sides fully developed with specific examples (e.g. Education Act 1988, Humanists UK, bishops in the Lords); sources of wisdom referenced; explicit weighing of arguments; clear, justified conclusion addressing whether a fully secular state is desirable.
Secure (9–12 marks): Both sides explained with some development; at least one specific reference; a conclusion reached.
Developing (5–8 marks): One side more developed than the other; limited specific references; partial conclusion.
Emerging (1–4 marks): Brief, one-sided or largely descriptive; few or no specific references. [15 marks including SPaG]

practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that include: a state-funded school run by or linked to a religious body (1 mark); which may prioritise admissions from its own faith community / teach from a faith perspective / appoint staff on religious grounds (1 mark). [2 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The constitutional title of the British Monarch, holding formal authority over the Church of England.
The process by which religion loses social significance and influence over public life, institutions and individuals.
A non-religious worldview that affirms human dignity and reason as the basis for ethics and meaning, without reference to the supernatural.
A state-funded school run by or linked to a religious body, which may prioritise admissions from its own faith community and teach from a faith perspective.
The deliberate ending of a person's life to relieve suffering, sometimes called assisted dying.
The right of individuals to make their own decisions about their lives and bodies, a key principle in secular ethics.
The use of technology to alter genetic material, including screening embryos, gene therapy, and selecting traits in unborn children.
